title: The Contaminated Arm

scenario.situation: A four-week promo test concluded with treatment showing +14% revenue versus control. The team is ready to roll out the promo company-wide.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The Growth team calls the promo a winner and wants to schedule the full launch for next sprint.
scenario.question: Is the +14% lift real, or is something else driving it?

decisions.prompt: The Growth team wants to confirm the win and move fast. How do you frame your investigation before signing off?

options.label: Validate the overall lift number
options.detail: Re-run the top-line revenue comparison between treatment and control to confirm the +14% figure is statistically significant.
options.consequence: The +14% holds up statistically — but you've only confirmed the number exists, not that the promo caused it. You've answered the wrong question.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on confirming the team's conclusion instead of interrogating whether the test was clean.

options.label: Audit arm balance and composition over time
options.detail: Check whether treatment and control arms remained comparable throughout the test — including who was assigned to each arm and when.
options.consequence: You pull arm membership by week and immediately see that a high-volume partner was onboarded directly into the treatment arm at the start of week two. The arms were not equivalent — a thread the top-line number never surfaces.

options.label: Segment the lift by promo engagement
options.detail: Compare revenue among users who actively engaged with the promo versus those who didn't.
options.consequence: Engaged users show even higher lift — but this is post-treatment self-selection. You've described what happened to people who used the promo, not whether the promo caused the aggregate gain.
options.divergenceCost: Introduced post-treatment selection bias by segmenting on engagement behavior.

options.label: Check if the test ran long enough for significance
options.detail: Audit the runtime and sample size against the original power calculation.
options.consequence: The test was adequately powered and ran its planned duration — so the lift looks credible. But you've checked the clock when you should have checked the guest list.
options.divergenceCost: Focused on test duration mechanics and missed the arm-contamination problem entirely.

decisions.prompt: You suspect the arms drifted. Which metric best reveals whether the lift is real or an artifact of who ended up in each arm?

artifact.title: Total revenue by arm — full test period
artifact.caption: Treatment outperforms control by +14% in aggregate. But does this reflect the promo's effect, or who was in each arm?

options.label: End-of-test revenue lift (aggregate)
options.detail: Use the final four-week revenue totals for treatment vs. control as the proof of lift.
options.consequence: The aggregate lift looks convincing, but it bundles together weeks before and after the new partner arrived. Any composition change is invisible inside this single number.
options.divergenceCost: Collapsed time into a single aggregate and hid the mid-test composition shift.

options.label: Week-over-week revenue per arm, with pre-period baseline
options.detail: Plot average revenue per partner by arm for each week of the test, including the two pre-test weeks to confirm arms were balanced at the start.
options.consequence: The pre-period lines are nearly identical — arms were balanced at launch. Then in week two, treatment revenue jumps sharply while control stays flat. That's exactly when the high-volume partner was onboarded into treatment. The promo's own signal, stripped of that partner, is indistinguishable from zero.

artifact.title: Avg revenue per partner by arm — pre-period and weekly
artifact.caption: Arms track closely in pre-period and week 1. Treatment spikes in week 2 — the same week the high-volume partner was onboarded into treatment only. Stripped of that partner, treatment and control are flat.

decisions.prompt: The weekly view shows the lift traces to the new partner's arrival, not the promo timing. What do you tell the Growth team?

options.label: "The promo didn't work — the test was contaminated, cancel the launch."
options.detail: Declare the test invalid and recommend against rollout.
options.consequence: You've correctly identified a problem but overstepped: the promo may still have an effect — you just can't measure it from this test. Killing the launch without a path forward leaves value on the table and erodes trust.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a null result from inconclusive data and offered no path to an answer.

options.label: "Arm composition changed mid-test, so we can't attribute the lift to the promo — we need a clean re-run with locked arm membership before launching."
options.detail: Flag the contamination, explain what it means for the current result, and recommend a clean retest.
options.consequence: The Growth team understands why the current number is untrustworthy, and you've given them a concrete next step: re-run the test with arm membership frozen at launch. The promo's true effect remains an open, answerable question.

insight: The +14% lift was real as a number but spurious as a signal — it traced entirely to a high-volume partner landing in the treatment arm mid-test, not to the promo itself. The pre-period and week-one parity proved the arms started clean; the week-two divergence revealed the contamination. The lesson: arm balance must be monitored across time, not just certified at launch, because composition shifts that happen during a test are invisible in any end-state aggregate.
